passage: Siddiq chalked his hands and looked at the orange route on the gym wall. It was one grade harder than anything he had finished. Tariq, holding the rope below, called, "You sure?" Third try, he stopped to study the wall from the floor and saw a foothold he had ignored. On the fourth attempt he stretched, hung, wobbled and clipped the last bolt with shaking arms. His forearms burned. He was grinning anyway.

passage: In the carpentry workshop at the polytechnic, Chetan pinned a sheet of drawings above his bench: a dovetail joint, a difficult one for a first-year. Nirmala, the instructor, passed and raised an eyebrow. "That is above where you are." "That is why I picked it," Chetan said. The first joint gapped. The second split at the corner. He swept the offcuts into the bin and marked the saw line again, thinner this time. By closing time the fifth joint fit with a hairline gap. He held it to the light. Nirmala looked, tapped it with a knuckle and said, "Do the sixth tomorrow, and bring the failed ones too."

passage:
Indu: "Siddharth, you've fallen off that route six times."
Siddharth: (chalking his hands) "Seven, actually."
Indu: "The yellow route next to it is easy for you. Why not do that?"
Siddharth: "Because I can already do it. What's the point?"
Indu: "The point is you'd get to the top."
Siddharth: "And learn nothing. This one, I get to the third hold and my fingers slip. Last week I couldn't reach the second."
Indu: "Doesn't it annoy you, failing so much?"
Siddharth: "Of course it does. My arms are burning and I feel stupid. But that's how I know it's the right route."
Indu: "That's a strange way to be happy."
Siddharth: "Watch. Attempt eight." (He reaches the fourth hold before falling.) "See? Fourth!"

qa.q: How many times had Siddharth fallen off the route before attempt eight?
qa.a: Seven times.

qa.q: How does Siddharth feel about failing on the hard route?
qa.a: He feels annoyed and a bit stupid, with burning arms, but also satisfied because the struggle means he is learning.

qa.q: Why is choosing the harder route a good choice for Siddharth?
qa.a: It is just beyond his current skill, so each attempt pushes him further, as shown by reaching the fourth hold.

qa.q: How does Indu see Siddharth's choice?
qa.a: Indu finds it puzzling, even a strange way to be happy, since the easy yellow route would get him to the top.

grounding: A dialogue shows a learner picking a climbing route just beyond his skill and accepting frequent falls as the price of growth.

passage: I'm Chetan, and in my second year of engineering I joined the college's coding contest group. The easy problems I could solve in ten minutes, and it felt great. But our mentor, Ritu, gave me problems rated one level above me. Every week I failed most of them. I'd sit for an hour and get nothing, then read the solution and feel like an idiot. Some nights I wanted to go back to easy problems just to feel clever. Ritu said, "If you're solving everything, you're not learning anything." By the end of the year, the problems that once beat me were the easy ones. I still remember that uncomfortable, not-quite-there feeling. That's what growing felt like.

qa.q: How long did the easy problems take Chetan?
qa.a: Chetan could solve the easy problems in ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel after failing the harder problems?
qa.a: Chetan felt like an idiot and was tempted to go back to easy problems just to feel clever.

qa.q: What was wise about Ritu's choice of problems?
qa.a: Giving problems one level above Chetan's skill kept Chetan at the edge of ability, where frequent failure produces real growth.

qa.q: How might Ritu see Chetan's weekly failures?
qa.a: Ritu seems to see them as a sign of learning, not weakness, saying that solving everything means learning nothing.

grounding: A student recalls working on problems just above current skill and accepting frequent failure as the path to growth.

passage:
Swimming coach's note, university team, February.
Simran asked this month to move from the intermediate lane to the advanced one. She knew she would be the slowest there. In her first week she missed the interval times on almost every set and once had to hold the wall to catch her breath. She looked frustrated, and a teammate, Reena, asked if she wanted to go back. Simran said, "No. In the old lane I was comfortable. Here I'm learning." By week three she was making half the intervals. I have kept her in the advanced lane and adjusted two sets so she can finish them with good form.

qa.q: Which lane did Simran move to?
qa.a: Simran moved to the advanced lane.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling in her first week in the advanced lane?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and exhausted, missing intervals, but still chose the difficulty because she knew it meant learning.

qa.q: What did the coach do to support Simran's choice?
qa.a: The coach kept her in the advanced lane and adjusted two sets so she could finish with good form.

qa.q: How might Reena see Simran's decision to stay?
qa.a: Reena, who offered her a way back, might be surprised and come to admire her willingness to struggle.

grounding: A coach's note shows a learner choosing a lane just beyond her ability and accepting failure as the price of growth.

Tuesday night, hostel
Chose the hardest story in the anthology again, the one full of Sundarbans dialect. Darshan-da said I could take the easy school story and be done in a day. I said no, which I half regretted by 10 pm.
Translated one page in three hours. Read it aloud. It sounded like a railway announcement. Crossed out half. Tried the fisherman's lines four different ways; none of them sounded like a real fisherman.
Darshan's note in the margin of last week's page: "Better. Still stiff in the arguments."
Strangely, I'm not miserable. Frustrated, yes, but the itchy kind, like when a word is on the tip of your tongue. A month ago even this page would have been impossible.
Tomorrow: the argument scene again. Fail a bit better.
Arnab

qa.a: Three hours.

qa.a: Arnab picks the hard story instead of the easy one, reads drafts aloud, tries lines several ways and keeps going back to the weak scene.

qa.a: Darshan offered the easy story but keeps giving honest notes like "Better", so Darshan probably respects the choice while seeing the work is still stiff.
